representative_papers.abstract: This paper presents approximation algorithms of polynomial time complexity for two scheduling problems with precedence constraints: the MAXPROFIT problem (maximizing profit within a given processor time) and the MINTIME problem (minimizing time to achieve a minimum profit). The algorithms are applicable when the precedence graph is a forest (a collection of trees). For any given $0 < \epsilon < 1$, the algorithms produce solutions within $\epsilon$ relative error of the optimal. Specifically, the k-PROFIT algorithm achieves a $1/(1+k)$-approximation for MAXPROFIT in $O(kn^{k+2})$ time. When tasks are independent, the MAXPROFIT algorithm reduces to an approximation for the 0/1 knapsack problem. The work also establishes theoretical bounds on solution quality using profit density and subtree analysis.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The approximation algorithms are only valid when the precedence graph is a forest. For arbitrary precedence graphs, the heuristics fail to guarantee bounded approximation ratios, as counterexamples exist where the relative error exceeds any given $\epsilon > 0$. The approach relies heavily on tree-like structure, limiting applicability to more complex dependency patterns.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future research could extend these approximation techniques to general directed acyclic graphs beyond forests. Investigating approximation schemes for broader classes of precedence constraints, or developing randomized or adaptive heuristics for non-forest cases, would be valuable. Additionally, exploring practical implementations and empirical performance evaluation under real-world task dependencies remains an open direction.

representative_papers.abstract: We prove that if two smooth manifolds intersect transversally, then the method of alternating projections converges locally at a linear rate. We bound the speed of convergence in terms of the angle between the manifolds, which in turn we relate to the modulus of metric regularity for the intersection problem, a natural measure of conditioning. We discuss a variety of problem classes where the projections are computationally tractable, and we illustrate the method numerically on a problem of finding a low-rank solution of a matrix equation.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Our aim in this work is not to develop efficient numerical schemes. Indeed, even for the classical alternating projection method on subspaces many authors have observed the slow convergence of the raw method, and have experimented with enhancements. Our goal here is primarily to initiate a solid theoretical explanation for observed successes of heuristics based on nonconvex alternating projections.

representative_papers.abstract: We consider a class of queueing systems that consist of server pools in parallel and multiple customer classes. Customer service times are assumed to be exponentially distributed. We study the asymptotic behavior of these queueing systems in a heavy traffic regime known as the Halfin-Whitt many-server asymptotic regime. Our main contribution is a general framework for establishing state space collapse results in this regime for parallel server systems. State space collapse refers to a decrease in the dimension of the processes tracking the number of customers in each class waiting for service and the number of customers in each class being served by various server pools. We define and introduce a 'state space collapse' function, which governs the exact details of the state space collapse. We show that a state space collapse result holds in many-server heavy traffic if a corresponding deterministic hydrodynamic model satisfies a similar state space collapse condition. Unlike the single-server heavy traffic setting for multiclass queueing networks, our hydrodynamic model is different from the standard fluid model for many-server queues. Our methodology is similar in spirit to that in Bramson [Bramson, M. 1998. State space collapse with application to heavy traffic limits for multiclass queueing networks. Queueing Systems 30 89–148], which focuses on the single-server heavy traffic regime. We illustrate the applications of our results by establishing state space collapse results in many-server diffusion limits for V-model systems under static-buffer-priority policy and the threshold policy proposed in the literature.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The framework presented cannot be directly applied to queue-and-idleness-ratio (QIR) controls with general holding costs, as the SSC function under such policies does not satisfy Assumption 4.1 unless the holding cost is linear. Additionally, the results are limited to systems with exponential service times and do not extend to general service time distributions without further assumptions.
representative_papers.future_work_text: An interesting research direction is to generalize the approach used by Gurvich and Whitt [24] to a broader class of control policies beyond QIR. Further exploration into extending the framework to non-exponential service time distributions and more complex routing policies would enhance its applicability. Additionally, investigating the robustness of state space collapse under model misspecification or heterogeneous server pools remains an open area.

representative_papers.abstract: We consider a $GI / G / 1$ queueing system where the $n$ th arrival may renege if his service does not commence before an elapsed random time $Z_{n}$ . Results for the general case include relations analogous to Little's formula $L = \lambda W$ , an expression for the average fraction of customers who renege from the system, expressions for the waiting time distribution for all arrivals to the system, the waiting time distribution for arrivals who reach the server, the distribution for virtual waiting time in the queue, and the distribution of the steady-state number of customers in the system and the number of customers left in the system by a completed service. These expressions are written in terms of the distribution of the work seen by an arbitrary arrival to the system, and an integral equation for this distribution is given along with necessary and sufficient conditions for existence of the distribution. Solutions to the integral equation are found for a number of forms for customer interarrival, service, and reneging distributions, and we show how the previous results on the subject of queueing with reneging follow as special cases of our approach. Some past and potential applications of queues with reneging are also discussed.
representative_papers.limitation_text: In §§I-IV, we assume that a customer who reaches the server will necessarily complete his service, that is, will not renegel from the server. The case of reneging from the server is possible and is treated, for example, in [1], [4] and [5]. §V considers the form of the results of the earlier sections when reneging is allowed after service begins. Although a complete treatment of this case is not included, the approach for analysis is presented.

representative_papers.abstract: Waiting times for many kinds of events can be represented as first passage times for appropriate stochastic processes. This paper considers new better than used (NBU) stochastic processes on partially ordered separable Banach spaces, defined as processes with NBU first passage times to closed upper sets. Various equivalent conditions for a process to be NBU are derived. Some results can also characterize increasing hazard rate average (IHRA) processes. Examples include processes with shocks and recovery and processes with random repair times. Applications in reliability theory and other areas of probability are discussed.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The analysis assumes the state space is a separable Banach space with a norm topology, which may limit applicability to more general topological spaces. The results rely heavily on the structure of closed convex cones and partial ordering, potentially restricting extension to non-ordered or non-linear state spaces. Additionally, the focus on increasing processes means the findings may not apply directly to non-monotonic or oscillatory processes.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future research could extend the framework to non-increasing or non-monotonic processes, explore NBU properties in non-Banach or non-separable spaces, and investigate applications in dynamic systems with feedback loops. Further work might also generalize the results to broader classes of stochastic processes beyond those with right-continuous paths, and examine connections between NBU processes and other stochastic orderings in complex network models.

representative_papers.abstract: Motivated by applications in computer and communication systems, we consider a processor-sharing queue where the number of jobs served is not larger than $K$. We propose a measure-valued fluid model for this limited processor-sharing queue and show that there exists a unique associated fluid model solution. In addition, we show that this fluid model arises as the limit of a sequence of appropriately scaled processor-sharing queues.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The analysis requires the assumption that the service-time distribution is continuous, which limits applicability to discrete or mixed distributions. Additionally, the complexity of the endogenous arrival process dynamics presents significant technical challenges, particularly in establishing regularity under finite $K$.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future work includes studying diffusion limits for LPS queues, which will enable analytical results in steady state and provide insightful approximations for performance quantities. Further research may extend the framework to incorporate deadlines, impatience, and more complex scheduling policies.

representative_papers.abstract: We analyse the optimal ordering policy for impulse control of a one-product inventory system subject to a demand modelled by a diffusion process. The purpose is to minimize the expected discounted cost that includes a fixed set-up cost and linear costs of purchase, storage and shortage. The optimal cost is explicitly obtained as the smoothest solution of a Quasi-Variational Inequality derived from the optimal principle of Dynamic Programming. The optimal $(s,S)$ policy is determined as the unique solution of a system of algebraic equations.

Indeed, continuity of the second derivative of $u$ at the point $s$ would imply either $\alpha \sigma$ or $p - \alpha C = 0$ which contradicts the assumptions or leads to non-existence of a solution.
representative_papers.future_work_text: The paper discusses special cases (deterministic demand, average cost case) in §4, suggesting further exploration of extensions to more complex demand processes or multi-product systems.

representative_papers.abstract: The concept of an additivization of a nonadditive probability measure is introduced and studied. The relation to cooperative game theory is explored, and it is shown that, in many cases of interest, additivizations may be considered as a special type of semvalues. An additivization is defined as an operator from a Banach space of not-necessarily-additive measures into the subspace of additive ones, satisfying axiomatic requirements including linearity, monotonicity, projectivity, and consistency. The paper establishes that under certain conditions, such operators exist and are unique, particularly for specific classes of measures like those in dNA. The results connect with semivalues in game theory and provide a formal framework for replacing nonadditive measures with additive ones in decision-making contexts.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The analysis relies on the assumption of an admissible sequence of partitions, which is weaker than standardness but still imposes structural constraints on the algebra of events. The uniqueness of additivizations depends crucially on monotonicity, which may not hold in all practical scenarios. Additionally, the focus on continuous additivizations limits applicability to certain function spaces, and the results are primarily theoretical without empirical validation.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future research could explore the empirical validity of additivizations in behavioral decision-making contexts, especially under uncertainty. Extending the framework to include non-continuous or non-monotonic measures would broaden its applicability. Investigating computational methods for approximating additivizations in complex models and analyzing their sensitivity to partition choices are also promising directions. Furthermore, connecting the theory more explicitly with real-world decision problems involving ambiguity aversion remains an open challenge.

representative_papers.abstract: We consider the general class of discounted problems involving sequential decision making over an unbounded horizon. Under the assumptions of a finite set of policy alternatives at each decision time and costs that are eventually uniformly bounded by some exponential, existence of an optimal infinite horizon strategy is established. Moreover, it is shown that there is a finite horizon version whose first policy decision agrees with an infinite horizon optimal policy. Under the additional assumption that the infinite horizon optimal strategy is eventually cyclic, the stronger result follows that the infinite horizon optimal solution is unique for almost all interest rates and that therefore a planning horizon exists. Algorithmic implications are explored for a restricted subclass of these problems.
representative_papers.limitation_text: Difficulties can arise when there are multiple infinite horizon optima, as seen in examples where strategies alternate as optimal without stabilizing, preventing the existence of a planning horizon. The results depend on the uniqueness or early agreement of infinite horizon optimal strategies; without such conditions, eventual stability in initial policies cannot be guaranteed.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Further research could explore relaxing the assumptions of deterministic problem characteristics and uniform exponential bounds to include stochastic or more complex cost structures. Additionally, extending algorithmic methods to handle cases with multiple optimal strategies or non-cyclic infinite horizon solutions would enhance practical applicability.

citation_semantics.parsed_title: Robust optimization—Methodology and applications
citation_semantics.description: This paper is cited as a key reference for the robust optimization approach, which addresses uncertainty by finding a single solution that is feasible for all parameter realizations within a given set. This approach is presented as an alternative to stochastic optimization that is significantly more tractable.
citation_semantics.context: More recently, the robust optimization approach has been considered to address optimization under uncertainty and has been studied extensively (see Ben-Tal and Nemirovski [4, 5, 6], El Ghaoui and Lebret [17], Goldfarb and Iyengar [19], Bertsimas and Sim [11, 12]). In a robust optimization approach, the uncertain parameters are assumed to belong to some uncertainty set, and the goal is to construct a single (static) solution that is feasible for all possible realizations of the uncertain parameters from the set and optimizes the worst-case objective.

citation_semantics.parsed_title: On the power of robust solutions in two-stage stochastic and adaptive optimization problems
citation_semantics.description: The authors cite this work for its analysis on the performance of static robust solutions in two-stage stochastic problems, particularly for perfectly symmetric uncertainty sets. The current paper explicitly states it is a two-fold generalization of these results, extending them to more general convex sets and multistage problems.
citation_semantics.context: Bertsimas and Goyal [10] analyze the performance of static robust solution in two-stage stochastic problems for perfectly symmetric uncertainty sets such as ellipsoids and norm-balls. We consider a generalized notion of symmetry of a convex set introduced in Minkowski [25], where the symmetry of a convex set is a number between 0 and 1. The symmetry of a set being equal to one implies that it is perfectly symmetric (such as an ellipsoid). We show that the performance of the static robust and the finitely adaptable solutions for the corresponding two-stage and multistage stochastic optimization problems depends on the symmetry of the uncertainty set. This is a two-fold generalization of the results in Bertsimas and Goyal [10].

domain_snapshot.development_history: Early work in dynamic decision optimization focused on discrete-time Markov decision processes and classical stochastic control, where the main technical emphasis was on establishing optimality/sufficiency of Markov (state-feedback) policies and tractable characterizations of value functions. This matured into broader formulations that relax idealized assumptions: (i) continuous-time dynamics with random jump events (CTJMDPs), where policy classes must be re-examined under measurability, non-explosion, and marginal-consistency constraints; (ii) impulse control, moving beyond continuous control to discrete interventions with execution delays and random (possibly non-Markovian) coefficients, solved via probabilistic constructs such as Snell envelopes and reflected BSDEs rather than only PDE/HJB approaches; (iii) integration of risk and constraints through financial mathematics—scalarizations of multivariate risk measures under transaction costs and eligibility constraints—embedding capital requirements and dual representations into decision criteria; and (iv) system-level decision/equilibrium problems in networks, where fixed-point formulations with monotone maps and saturation nonlinearities represent capacity/solvency constraints and create coupled decision interactions. More recently, attention has expanded to decision objectives that are not simple expectations (e.g., tail- and count-based metrics such as “cardinality of upper average” used in network optimization), reflecting operational goals like limiting the number of severe outcomes rather than only their mean magnitude. Overall, the technical trajectory is from Markovian, expectation-based, single-agent optimization toward continuous-time, delayed/impulsive actions, coherent risk-aware objectives, and interconnected networked equilibria with non-smooth nonlinearities—at the cost of new pathologies (explosion, non-uniqueness, time-inconsistency) and heavier analytical machinery (duality, fixed points, BSDEs).

representative_papers.abstract: A new predictor-corrector interior point algorithm for solving monotone linear complementarity problems (LCP) is proposed, and it is shown to be superlinearly convergent with at least order 1.5, even if the LCP has no strictly complementary solution. Unlike the algorithm of Mizuno (1996), the fast local convergence is attained without any need for estimating the optimal partition. In the special case that a strictly complementary solution does exist, the order of convergence becomes quadratic. The proof relies on an investigation of the asymptotic behavior of first and second order derivatives associated with trajectories of weighted centers for monotone LCPs. The results are also used to study convergence and error bounds of three Tapia-type indicators.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The algorithm's performance is analyzed under the assumption that interior solutions exist, i.e., the set {(x, s) ∈ ℝ₊₊ⁿ × ℝ₊₊ⁿ | Qx + Rs = b} is nonempty. This condition ensures the existence of feasible interior points but may not hold for all instances of monotone LCPs. Additionally, the analysis focuses on the asymptotic behavior near the solution set, which may limit practical applicability when iterates are far from optimality.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future research could extend the algorithm to broader classes of LCPs beyond monotone problems, such as sufficient or P* (κ)-LCPs. Investigating practical implementations with adaptive weight updates and computational efficiency improvements would enhance real-world applicability. Further exploration of Tapia-type indicators' behavior in non-strictly complementary settings could yield better early termination criteria.

representative_papers.abstract: We present a perturbation theory for finite dimensional optimization problems subject to abstract constraints satisfying a second order regularity condition. This is a technical condition that is always satisfied in the case of semi-definite optimization. We derive Lipschitz and Hölder expansions of approximate optimal solutions, under a directional constraint qualification hypothesis and various second order sufficient conditions that take into account the curvature of the set defining the constraints of the problem. We show how the theory applies to semi-infinite programs in which the contact set is a smooth manifold and the quadratic growth condition in the constraint space holds, and discuss the differentiability of metric projections as well as the Moreau-Yosida regularization. Finally we show how the theory applies to semi-definite optimization.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The theory relies on a directional constraint qualification and second order sufficient conditions that depend on the curvature of the constraint set K. The results are limited to cases where inner second order regularity holds, and may not apply when the set of Lagrange multipliers is empty or when the curvature effects are too complex to be captured by the current framework. Additionally, the analysis assumes twice continuously differentiable mappings f and G, restricting applicability to smooth problems.

representative_papers.abstract: We demonstrate the impossibility of strongly polynomial algorithms for the allocation problem, in the comparison model and in the algebraic tree computation model, that follow from lower bound results. Consequently, there are no strongly polynomial algorithms for nonlinear (concave) separable optimization over a totally unimodular constraint matrix. This is in contrast to the case when the objective is linear. We present scaling-based algorithms that use a greedy algorithm as a subroutine. The algorithms are polynomial for the allocation problem and its extensions and are also optimal for the simple allocation problem and the generalized upper bounds allocation problem, in that the complexity meets the lower bound derived from the comparison model. For other extensions of the allocation problem the scaling-based algorithms presented here are the fastest known. These algorithms are also polynomial time algorithms for solving with ε accuracy the allocation problem and its extension in continuous variables.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The dependence on log(B/ε) in the running time of the algorithm cannot be removed even for the simple case of the allocation problem and hence for the general problem as well (with the possible exception of quadratic objective function). This lower bound result holds for both the comparison model and the algebraic computation tree model with the four arithmetic operations +, -, ·, ÷, and comparisons. It holds even if the floor operation is permitted. Since the simple allocation problem is a special case of separable concave maximization problems over totally unimodular constraint matrices or over polymatroidal constraints, then in particular all allocation problems and nonlinear convex network flow problems cannot be solved in strongly polynomial time.
representative_papers.future_work_text: The paper concludes with some open questions regarding the potential for further improvements in algorithmic efficiency and the exploration of additional classes of nonlinear optimization problems that may admit strongly polynomial solutions under specific structural assumptions. Future work could also investigate practical implementations of the proposed scaling algorithms and their performance on real-world instances of allocation problems.

domain_snapshot.development_history: The technical trajectory toward approximation in multi-objective nonlinear optimization (MONO) has evolved through three interacting threads reflected by the representative works. First, foundational progress focused on geometric and conditioning-based surrogates that make feasibility and robustness quantifiable without heavy dependence on data scaling or instance-specific tuning. This is exemplified by the move toward intrinsic, geometry-driven condition measures (e.g., data-independent distance-to-infeasibility concepts for conic systems), which supplies optimization algorithms with approximation-relevant certificates (how far from infeasible/ill-posed a formulation is) that can be used to stabilize multi-objective scalarizations and constraint-handling schemes. Second, algorithmic approximation shifted from smooth settings to nonsmooth and nonconvex structures via composite modeling (notably DC programming), where approximate stationarity notions (e.g., approximate Clarke stationarity) provide practical termination criteria and approximation guarantees when exact optimality is unattainable. The introduction of bundle-based proximal frameworks with explicit escape mechanisms highlights a present-day emphasis on reliably obtaining “good enough” stationary solutions in hard nonlinear landscapes. Third, interior-point theory for linearly constrained convex programming advanced the understanding of path-following approximations: generalized central paths and their convergence analysis provide a principled way to generate sequences of approximate solutions (primal-dual iterates) with controllable accuracy, which is a key enabler for scalable approximations when MONO is tackled through convex scalarizations or barrier-based methods. Across these threads, the field has moved from problem-specific approximation ratios and discrete combinatorial approximations toward unified notions of approximate feasibility/stationarity/trajectory convergence that can be composed into modern MONO pipelines; however, bridging these guarantees into genuinely multi-objective, nonlinear, and nonsmooth settings remains incomplete.

representative_papers.abstract: In this paper, we consider a semi-infinite relaxation of mixed-integer linear programs. We show that minimal valid inequalities for this relaxation correspond to maximal lattice-free convex sets, and that they arise from nonnegative, piecewise linear, positively homogeneous, convex functions. The main result establishes a one-to-one correspondence between minimal valid functions and full-dimensional maximal lattice-free convex sets containing the fractional vector f. This characterization provides a geometric understanding of cutting planes in integer programming and has applications in deriving strong valid inequalities for mixed-integer programs.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The analysis is restricted to the semi-infinite relaxation where nonbasic variables are continuous and only finitely many are nonzero. The results rely on the assumption that f is not integral, and the function ψ may be infinite or discontinuous at certain points. The characterization applies specifically to minimal valid inequalities, which limits its direct use for non-minimal cuts. Additionally, while the paper establishes theoretical connections, computational implementation remains challenging due to the infinite-dimensional nature of the problem.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future work includes extending the characterization to handle more general classes of integer programs beyond the semi-infinite relaxation, developing efficient algorithms to compute minimal valid inequalities for practical instances, and exploring the structure of non-minimal valid inequalities. Further research could investigate the computational performance of cuts derived from maximal lattice-free sets in real-world optimization problems, as well as the extension of these results to multi-row and multi-commodity settings.

domain_snapshot.development_history: Early work around lattice-free convexity in integer optimization focused on identifying and exploiting convex sets with no interior integer points as certificates for cutting planes (intersection cuts, split cuts). This matured into a structural program: characterize maximal (and integral) lattice-free polyhedra, first cleanly in low dimensions (notably a detailed dimension-3 taxonomy of maximality notions), and use these structures to understand what kinds of cuts can arise from lattice-free geometry. In parallel, researchers developed complexity/strength perspectives: rank measures for closures (split, multibranch, lattice-free) were related to integrality gaps, demonstrating that even for structured families (packing/covering), many closure iterations may be necessary—highlighting inherent limits of projection-free strengthening via standard disjunctions. More recently, the technical toolkit expanded in two directions: (i) reverse convex sets frameworks that unify intersection-disjunction reasoning for sets defined as polyhedron minus an open convex region, aligning with bilevel/polynomial models and broadening the geometric objects from pure lattice-free polyhedra to reverse convex geometries; and (ii) function-based viewpoints (cut-generating functions / Gomory–Johnson theory), where approximation and density results established that extreme functions are dense among minimal functions in all dimensions, providing a constructive approximation pathway for strong cuts. Collectively, the field has progressed from (a) geometric existence/characterization of lattice-free objects, to (b) quantitative limits via rank lower bounds, to (c) generalized modeling contexts (reverse convexity) and (d) approximation/constructive mechanisms for generating strong valid inequalities—yet with a persistent gap between structural theory and practical, projection-aware algorithms for projecting lattice-free polytopes without interior lattice points.

representative_papers.abstract: This paper develops a value theory for voting games where a significant portion of the vote is controlled by a few major players, while the remainder is distributed among a continuous infinity of individually insignificant minor players, referred to collectively as an 'ocean'. The authors define the value of such 'oceanic games' using a pivotal player approach based on random orderings, ensuring continuity with finite approximants. They derive explicit expressions for player values, particularly in 'interior' games where the ocean alone forms a winning coalition, and analyze properties of the value solution, including its dependence on the majority quota. The oceanic value is shown to be related to the derivative of the expected pivot location, and a theorem establishes that average values over all quotas equal each player's weight fraction.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The analysis assumes a perfectly symmetric and homogeneous ocean with no internal structure or cohesion, which may not reflect real-world scenarios where minor players exhibit some degree of organization or clustering. Additionally, the model relies on idealized random ordering assumptions that may not hold under practical voting dynamics.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future research could extend the model to include structured oceans with subgroups or hierarchies, explore non-symmetric distributions of power among major players, and investigate applications in political economics, resource allocation, and large-scale decision-making systems where continuum models are relevant.

representative_papers.abstract: This paper analyzes the behavior of weighted majority games when a block of votes is broken up and distributed among a large number of players. It demonstrates that as the size of the largest fragment tends to zero, the value of the game to the other players converges to a limit. An explicit expression for this limit is provided in Theorem 1 and its corollaries. The study focuses on finite-person games and establishes a limit theorem for the Shapley values under conditions where minor players' weights become arbitrarily small while their total weight remains constant.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The analysis is restricted to games with finite carriers and does not extend the 'value' concept to games without finite carriers. The results are derived under specific assumptions about the distribution of minor player weights and do not address more complex or asymmetric configurations beyond the given framework.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future work will explore infinite-person games, including those with an uncountable 'ocean' of players, countably infinite games, bi- and multi-camera games, and numerical computations of values for specific large games. Extensions to other classes of games and generalizations of the current results are also anticipated.

representative_papers.abstract: Existing notions of proximity of information fail to satisfy desired continuity properties of equilibria in games with incomplete information. We demonstrate this failure and propose a topology on information structures which is the minimal one that satisfies those continuity requirements. This topology is defined in terms of the common belief players have about the proximity of each player's information. Two information structures are close iff, for any game over the state space, an equilibrium of the game under one information structure can, by changing it a little, be made an almost equilibrium under the other information structure. The notion of common belief is central to our definition, and we show that the resulting topology is the coarsest one ensuring continuity of equilibria.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The paper restricts attention to purely atomic σ-fields or countable partitions to ensure existence of equilibria and avoid complex mathematical analysis. This limits generality, as non-atomic information structures are excluded. Additionally, the focus on ex-post payoffs for 'almost equilibrium' may not capture all relevant strategic behaviors in more complex settings.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Further research is needed to explore the relationship between the proposed topology and existing notions of proximity in works like Milgrom and Weber (1985) and Kajii and Morris (1994), especially when prior probabilities vary. Extending the framework to non-atomic information structures and investigating applications in dynamic games or repeated interactions would also be valuable.

representative_papers.abstract: This paper proves that in games with a finite number of players and a finite number of moves, if each player observes a private information random variable with an atomless distribution independent of the observations and payoffs of other players, then a pure-strategy equilibrium exists. The authors generalize this result to cases where a player's payoff may be correlated with their private observation. They show that every mixed-strategy equilibrium has a corresponding pure-strategy equilibrium yielding the same expected payoff. Examples illustrate the necessity of the assumptions, highlighting conditions under which pure-strategy equilibria exist or fail.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The existence of pure-strategy equilibria relies on strong assumptions: private information variables must have atomless distributions and be independent of other players' observations and payoffs. The results do not extend to cases where these independence or atomlessness conditions are violated, as demonstrated by counterexamples in Section 4.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future research could explore weaker conditions under which pure-strategy equilibria exist, particularly in settings with correlated information or non-atomless distributions. Additionally, extending the analysis to approximate pure-strategy equilibria in broader contexts—such as large games or continuous strategy spaces—remains an open direction.

representative_papers.abstract: An elementary proof, based on linear duality, is provided for the existence of correlated equilibria in finite games. The existence result is then extended to infinite games, including some that possess no Nash equilibria. For countably additive correlated equilibria, existence is established when payoff functions are continuous and strategy spaces are compact Hausdorff. Proofs rely on product compactness (e.g., Tychonoff's Theorem) rather than fixed-point theorems.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The existence of countably additive correlated equilibria is guaranteed only under continuity of payoff functions and compactness of strategy spaces; without these conditions, such equilibria may not exist, as demonstrated by examples with discontinuous payoffs.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Further exploration of correlated equilibria in games with non-compact or non-Hausdorff strategy spaces, and investigation of computational aspects of finding correlated equilibria in infinite games, remain open directions.

representative_papers.abstract: We prove that every multiplayer perfect-information game with bounded and lower-semicontinuous payoffs admits a subgame-perfect ε-equilibrium in pure strategies. This result complements Example 3 in Solan and Vieille [Solan, E., N. Vieille. 2003. Deterministic multi-player Dynkin games. J. Math. Econom. 39 911-929], which shows that a subgame-perfect ε-equilibrium in pure strategies need not exist when the payoffs are not lower-semicontinuous. In addition, if the range of payoffs is finite, we characterize in the form of a Folk Theorem the set of all plays and payoffs that are induced by subgame-perfect 0-equilibria in pure strategies.
representative_papers.future_work_text: In §4.2 we point at another possible application of our technique. Recently, Purves and Sudderth [14], using ideas different from ours, complemented our result by showing that a subgame perfect ε-equilibrium exists if the payoff processes are bounded and upper-semicontinuous.

representative_papers.abstract: We derive versions of known results dealing with core, equilibria and Shapley-values of cooperative games in the case of cooperative fuzzy games, i.e., games defined on fuzzy subsets of the set of $n$ players. A fuzzy coalition is an $n$ -vector $\tau = (\tau_{i})$ associating with each player $i$ his "rate of participation" $\tau_{i} \in [0,1]$ in the fuzzy coalition and the real number $v(\cdot)$ is the coalition worth, assumed to be positively homogeneous. If also $v$ is superadditive, or equivalently concave, the fuzzy game with side payments has a nonempty core. Associated with the coalition-worth function for any ordinary game with side payments is a fuzzy extension thereof, viz., the fuzzy game whose coalition-worth function is the least positively-homogeneous superadditive function majorizing the coalition-worth function of the original game. The fuzzy extension always has a nonempty core. Moreover, if the original game has a nonempty core, it coincides with that of its fuzzy extension. Analogous results are established for games without side payments. An axiomatization of "values" of fuzzy games with side payments is also given. The results are applied to show that the set of Walras equilibria coincides with the fuzzy core of an economy.

representative_papers.abstract: We develop first-order smoothing techniques for saddle-point problems that arise in finding a Nash equilibrium of sequential games. The crux of our work is a construction of suitable prox-functions for a certain class of polytopes that encode the sequential nature of the game. We also introduce heuristics that significantly speed up the algorithm, and decomposed game representations that reduce the memory requirements, enabling the application of the techniques to drastically larger games. An implementation based on our smoothing techniques computes approximate Nash equilibria for games that are more than four orders of magnitude larger than what prior approaches can handle. Finally, we show near-linear further speedups from parallelization.
representative_papers.future_work_text: The paper summarizes main conclusions and discusses ideas for future work, including potential extensions of the smoothing techniques to broader classes of games and further optimization of computational efficiency through advanced parallelization and algorithmic refinements.

representative_papers.abstract: This paper is the first of two devoted to the study of egalitarian solutions for nontransferable utility (NTU) games with a large number of players. It focuses on constructing egalitarian solutions in the limit case of a continuum of players, building on the Potential concept introduced by Hart and Mas-Colell (1989) and employing partial differential equations techniques. A variational problem is associated with the egalitarian solutions, generalizing the diagonal principle of Aumann and Shapley (1974) to the NTU context. The analysis relies on a model with finitely many player types and assumes standard properties such as convexity, closedness, and superadditivity of feasible payoff sets. The framework allows for economic interpretations and provides a foundation for analyzing large-scale cooperative games through continuous approximations.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The analysis is restricted to games with finitely many player types and does not consider boundary cases where some player types have zero mass. The results depend on assumptions about the structure of the game form, particularly the boundedness of support vectors (A.4), which may exclude certain economically relevant configurations. Additionally, the continuum model requires validation via asymptotic analysis of finite games, which is addressed in the companion paper but not fully developed here.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future work includes extending the theory to handle boundary cases and unbounded support vectors, validating the continuum model through asymptotic analysis of finite games, and applying the framework to concrete economic models such as markets with heterogeneous agents. Further exploration of the relationship between egalitarian solutions and competitive equilibria—particularly in large economies—is also anticipated, building on the equivalence theorems initiated in Hart and Mas-Colell (1996).

representative_papers.abstract: We study from a complexity theoretic standpoint the various solution concepts arising in cooperative game theory. We use as a vehicle for this study a game in which the players are nodes of a graph with weights on the edges, and the value of a coalition is determined by the total weight of the edges contained in it. The Shapley value is always easy to compute. The core is easy to characterize when the game is convex, and is intractable (NP-complete) otherwise. Similar results are shown for the kernel, the nucleolus, the ε-core, and the bargaining set. As for the von Neumann-Morgenstern solution, we point out that its existence may not even be decidable. Many of these results generalize to the case in which the game is presented by a hypergraph with edges of size k > 2.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The analysis focuses on games defined by weighted graphs or hypergraphs, limiting generalization to other types of cooperative games. The computational complexity results depend heavily on the structure of the graph and the sign of edge weights, particularly assuming integer weights and undirected graphs. Extensions to more complex or arbitrary coalition structures are not fully explored.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future work could extend the analysis to more general classes of games beyond graph-based models, including those with arbitrary coalition values or non-additive structures. Investigating the complexity of solution concepts in stochastic or dynamic cooperative settings, as well as exploring approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems like the core or bargaining set, would also be valuable directions.

representative_papers.abstract: Cores of games of the form $f \circ \mu$, where $\mu$ is a vector of nonatomic measures and $f(z) = \max \{ \langle c, x \rangle \mid xA \leqslant z, x \geqslant 0 \}$ or equivalently $f(z) = \min \langle z, a^i \rangle$, are described in terms of $\mu$ and the data defining $f$. The main result shows that every measure in the core is of the form $\lambda = \langle y, \mu \rangle$, where $y$ is an optimal solution to the dual problem. A general condition is also established implying that each measure in the core is a linear combination of a fixed finite set of nonatomic measures.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The analysis assumes the game is of the specific form $f \circ \mu$ with $f$ being the minimum of linear functions, limiting applicability to broader classes of nonatomic games. Additionally, the results rely on the convexity of the range of nonatomic vector measures via Lyapunov's theorem, which may not extend to non-convex settings.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future research could extend these results to more general classes of nonatomic games beyond linear production forms, explore core stability under perturbations of the measure space, and investigate asymptotic properties in non-atomic markets with heterogeneous agents or incomplete information.

representative_papers.abstract: An economic production game is treated, in which players pool resources to produce finished goods which can be sold at a given market price. The production process is linear, so that the characteristic function can be obtained by solving linear programs. Duality theory of linear programming is used to obtain equilibrium price vectors and to prove the non-emptiness of the core. Under replication, it is shown that, in the non-degenerate case, the core converges finitely to the set of competitive equilibria; a counter-example shows that this is not true in the degenerate case (i.e., only convergence in the limit can be guaranteed).

domain_snapshot.development_history: Early work in game equilibrium and optimization algorithms emphasized existence/uniqueness of equilibria and algorithmic computation in structured settings (e.g., potential games, routing/congestion with simple costs), alongside foundational cooperative-solution computation (e.g., bargaining/coalitional stability notions). The field then shifted toward quantifying inefficiency via worst-case equilibrium metrics such as Price of Anarchy (PoA), with tight bounds established for broad classes (e.g., affine-delay congestion games) and increasing attention to how network topology (e.g., series-parallel vs. general graphs) changes attainable guarantees. More recent work refines this inefficiency analysis from static worst-case statements to parametric/structural characterizations: PoA as a function of demand and the geometry of breakpoints in routing games; topology-restricted PoA improvements in series-parallel networks; and bilevel/leader–follower equilibrium models where strategic leaders induce congestion-coupled follower equilibria (Stackelberg pricing with nonatomic congestion). In parallel, equilibrium concepts have been extended to better capture dynamic/absorbing interactions (e.g., absorption paths in quitting games bridging discrete and continuous-time views), while cooperative-game optimization has advanced to more scalable computation of refined solutions (e.g., pseudo-polynomial-time nucleolus computation for weighted voting games). Overall, the technical arc moves from (i) equilibrium existence and computability in idealized models, to (ii) sharp inefficiency bounds under increasing realism and structural constraints, to (iii) parametric/dynamic/bilevel models and more scalable algorithms for refined solution concepts, with limitations emerging when relaxing cost structure beyond affine/linear forms.

representative_papers.l2_label: Cutting Plane Methods and Decomposition Optimization
representative_papers.abstract: We propose a cutting plane algorithm for mixed 0-1 programs based on a family of polyhedra which strengthen the usual LP relaxation. We show how to generate a facet of a polyhedron in this family which is most violated by the current fractional point. This cut is found through the solution of a linear program that has about twice the size of the usual LP relaxation. A lifting step is used to reduce the size of the LP's needed to generate the cuts. An additional strengthening step suggested by Balas and Jeroslow is then applied. We report our computational experience with a preliminary version of the algorithm. This approach is related to the work of Balas on disjunctive programming, the matrix cone relaxations of Lovász and Schrijver and the hierarchy of relaxations of Sherali and Adams.

representative_papers.abstract: Integer programs defined by two equations with two free integer variables and nonnegative continuous variables have three types of nontrivial facets: split, triangle or quadrilateral inequalities. In this paper, we compare the strength of these three families of inequalities. In particular we study how well each family approximates the integer hull. We show that, in a well defined sense, triangle inequalities provide a good approximation of the integer hull. The same statement holds for quadrilateral inequalities. On the other hand, the approximation produced by split inequalities may be arbitrarily bad.

representative_papers.l2_label: Cutting Plane Methods and Decomposition Optimization
representative_papers.abstract: Given a graph $G = [V, E]$ with positive edge weights, the max-cut problem is to find a cut in $G$ such that the sum of the weights of the edges of this cut is as large as possible. Let $\mathcal{G}(K)$ be the class of graphs whose longest odd cycle is not longer than $2K + 1$ , where $K$ is a nonnegative integer independent of the number $n$ of nodes of $G$ . We present an $O(n^{4K})$ algorithm for the max-cut problem for graphs in $\mathcal{G}(K)$ . The algorithm is recursive and is based on some properties of longest and longest odd cycles of graphs.
representative_papers.limitation_text: While results of this type are of practical interest only for small values of $K$, they are of theoretical significance in sharpening the delineation (if any) between the classes P and NP. Of course, it would be inefficient to develop results of this type problem-by-problem individually.
representative_papers.future_work_text: it would be very nice to have a general result of the type: If a combinatorial optimization problem is easy for bipartite graphs, then it is also easy for $\mathcal{G}(K)$ for every fixed $K$. We don't, however, know whether this result is true; for example, we don't know if it is true for the minimum cardinality coloring problem of the vertices of a graph, which is a trivial problem for bipartite graphs. This study of the max-cut problem was undertaken, in part, to see if a general methodology could be developed for a large class of combinatorial optimization problems. While the design of our max-cut algorithm is based on an idea developed in [8], it requires deeper theorems on the intersections of longest cycles in a graph; these may be of interest in their own right. It still remains open whether the approach can be extended to a large class of problems.

representative_papers.abstract: We introduce and study an eigenvalue upper bound φ(G) on the maximum cut mc(G) of a weighted graph. The function φ(G) has several interesting properties that resemble the behaviour of mc(G). We show that φ is subadditive with respect to amalgam, and additive with respect to disjoint sum and 1-sum. We prove that φ(G) is never worse than 1.131mc(G) for a planar, or more generally, a weakly bipartite graph with nonnegative edge weights. We give a dual characterization of φ(G), and show that φ(G) is computable in polynomial time with arbitrary precision.

representative_papers.l2_label: Cutting Plane Methods and Decomposition Optimization
representative_papers.abstract: Disjunctive cuts for Mixed-Integer Linear Programs (MIPs) were introduced by Egon Balas in the late 1970s and have been successfully exploited in practice since the late 1990s. In this paper we investigate the main ingredients of a disjunctive cut separation procedure, and analyze their impact on the quality of the root-node bound for a set of instances taken from MIPLIB library. We compare alternative normalization conditions, and try to better understand their role. In particular, we point out that constraints that become redundant (because of the disjunction used) can produce over-weak cuts, and analyze this property with respect to the normalization used. Finally, we introduce a new normalization condition and analyze its theoretical properties and computational behavior. Along the way, we make use of a number of small numerical examples to illustrate some basic (and often misinterpreted) disjunctive programming features.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The study focuses on root-node performance and does not consider the impact of disjunctive cuts throughout the entire branch-and-bound tree. Additionally, no a posteriori cut strengthening is applied unless explicitly stated, which may limit the observed improvement in bound quality. The analysis is primarily based on MIPLIB instances, potentially limiting generalizability to other problem classes.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future work includes extending the analysis to deeper levels of the branch-and-bound tree, investigating the integration of the proposed normalization with advanced cut strengthening techniques, and testing the new normalization on broader classes of MIPs beyond set-covering problems. Further theoretical exploration of the relationship between disjunction structure, constraint redundancy, and cut strength is also warranted.

representative_papers.abstract: A simple algorithm is described for constructing a maximum packing of cuts directed away from a distinguished vertex, called the root, in a directed graph, each of whose edges has a non-negative weight, and it is shown that the maximum packing value is equal to the weight of a minimum-weight spanning arborescence directed away from the root. The algorithm assigns nonnegative weights to rooted directed cuts sequentially, never revising prior assignments, and terminates when either an empty cut is found (indicating infinite packing value) or a single component remains (indicating optimality). The method is a modification of Edmonds' algorithm for optimum branchings and guarantees an integer solution vector y whose sum equals the minimum-weight arborescence weight.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The algorithm may fail to detect the absence of a spanning arborescence rooted at r if not initially checked; however, this case is detected during execution. The method assumes non-negative edge weights and does not address graphs with negative weights. Additionally, while the algorithm constructs a maximum packing, it does not explicitly handle cases where multiple edges exist between vertices unless simplified by taking minimum weights.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Further research could extend the algorithm to handle graphs with negative edge weights or incorporate dynamic updates for real-time applications. Investigating parallelization of the algorithm for large-scale graphs would also be valuable. Additionally, exploring connections to other combinatorial optimization problems involving blocking pairs of polyhedra or anti-blocking structures could yield deeper theoretical insights.

We prove that the rate of convergence of the second method is optimal uniformly in the number of variables. We present a modification of the second method. In this modified version each test point satisfies an approximate centering condition. We also use the standard strategy for updating approximate Hessians of the logarithmic barrier function. We prove that the rate of convergence of the modified scheme remains optimal and demonstrate that the number of Newton steps in the auxiliary minimization processes is bounded by an absolute constant. We also show that the approximate Hessian strategy significantly improves the total arithmetical complexity of the method.

domain_snapshot.development_history: Early work in this domain emphasized decomposition-centric exact methods where cutting planes are embedded into iterative improvement frameworks. A representative example is Integral Simplex Using Decomposition with Primal Cutting Planes (2017), which integrates primal cut generation into a decomposition-based integral simplex approach for set partitioning, reflecting a focus on practical algorithm engineering: generate violated inequalities from incumbent structure, tighten the master, and iterate. By 2019, the field broadened beyond classical separation-at-vertices toward alternative geometric primitives and algorithmic goals. Projective Cutting-Planes (2019) reframes cut generation around projection/pierce points from an interior feasible point along directions, emphasizing features like producing feasible solutions throughout and eliminating variables—highlighting an evolution from purely tightening LP relaxations to simultaneously managing feasibility, guidance, and structure exploitation. In parallel, approximation and integrality-gap research (e.g., tight approximation for linear 3-cut (2019) and improved integrality gap constructions for multiway cut (2020)) sharpened understanding of when relaxations and cut families fundamentally succeed or fail, thereby informing which inequalities or formulations are worth pursuing. The most recent trend (2021) moves toward combinatorial and data-structure-driven cut-and-lift mechanisms: a BDD-based encoding is used to exploit 0-1 structure for systematic lifting and cut derivation, aligning with a broader shift to harness problem structure (logic/automata/diagrams) for stronger cuts and better separability. Across this timeline, the technical evolution is from decomposition + classical cutting planes, to geometry-aware and feasibility-aware cutting-plane variants, to structure-exploiting combinatorial cut-and-lift frameworks, with integrality-gap/approximation insights increasingly guiding which relaxation-tightening strategies are likely to pay off.

Projective Cutting-Planes (2019) reframes cut generation around projection/pierce points from an interior feasible point along directions, emphasizing features like producing feasible solutions throughout and eliminating variables—highlighting an evolution from purely tightening LP relaxations to simultaneously managing feasibility, guidance, and structure exploitation. In parallel, approximation and integrality-gap research (e.g., tight approximation for linear 3-cut (2019) and improved integrality gap constructions for multiway cut (2020)) sharpened understanding of when relaxations and cut families fundamentally succeed or fail, thereby informing which inequalities or formulations are worth pursuing. The most recent trend (2021) moves toward combinatorial and data-structure-driven cut-and-lift mechanisms: a BDD-based encoding is used to exploit 0-1 structure for systematic lifting and cut derivation, aligning with a broader shift to harness problem structure (logic/automata/diagrams) for stronger cuts and better separability. Across this timeline, the technical evolution is from decomposition + classical cutting planes, to geometry-aware and feasibility-aware cutting-plane variants, to structure-exploiting combinatorial cut-and-lift frameworks, with integrality-gap/approximation insights increasingly guiding which relaxation-tightening strategies are likely to pay off.

By using the equivalent node-packing problem derived from the intersection graph associated with the problem, it is shown that cliques in the intersection graph provide a first set of facets, while odd cycles without chords yield a second set. A strong geometric property of this latter set of facets is also exhibited.

representative_papers.abstract: The role of 0-1 programming problems having monotone or regular feasible sets was pointed out in [6]. The solution sets of covering and of knapsack problems are examples of monotone and of regular sets respectively. Some connections are established between prime implicants of a monotone or a regular Boolean function β on the one hand, and facets of the convex hull H of the zeros of β on the other. In particular (Corollary 2) a necessary and sufficient condition is given for a constraint of a covering problem to be a facet of the corresponding integer polyhedron. For any prime implicant P of β, a nonempty family F(P) of facets of H is constructed. Proposition 17 gives easy-to-determine sharp upper bounds for the coefficients of these facets when β is regular. A special class of prime implicants is described for regular functions and it is shown that for any P in this class, F(P) consists of one facet of H, and this facet has 0-1 coefficients. Every nontrivial facet of H with 0-1 coefficients is obtained from this class.

representative_papers.abstract: The cut polytope $P_{\mathbf{C}}(G)$ of a graph $G = (V, E)$ is the convex hull of the incidence vectors of all edge sets of cuts of $G$. We show some classes of facet-defining inequalities of $P_{\mathbf{C}}(G)$. In particular, we show that inequalities associated with chordless cycles define facets of this polytope; moreover, for these inequalities a polynomial algorithm to solve the separation problem is presented. We characterize the facet defining inequalities of $P_{\mathbf{C}}(G)$ if $G$ is not contractible to $K_5$. We give a simple characterization of adjacency in $P_{\mathbf{C}}(G)$ and prove that for complete graphs this polytope has diameter one and that $P_{\mathbf{C}}(G)$ has the Hirsch property. A relationship between $P_{\mathbf{C}}(G)$ and the convex hull of incidence vectors of balancing edge sets of a signed graph is studied.

representative_papers.abstract: We consider a binary integer programming formulation (VP) for the weighted vertex packing problem in a simple graph. A sufficient "local" optimality condition for (VP) is given and this result is used to derive relations between (VP) and the linear program (VLP) obtained by deleting the integrality restrictions in (VP). Our most striking result is that those variables which assume binary values in an optimum (VLP) solution retain the same values in an optimum (VP) solution. This result is of interest because variables are $(0, \frac{1}{2}, 1)$ valued in basic feasible solutions to (VLP) and (VLP) can be solved by a "good" algorithm. This relationship and other optimality conditions are incorporated into an implicit enumeration algorithm for solving (VP). Some computational experience is reported.

representative_papers.abstract: This paper provides a detailed analysis of integral polyhedra in three-dimensional space, focusing on convex polyhedra whose vertices are lattice points and which contain no other lattice points. The study is based on an unpublished theorem by Roger Howe, which shows that any integral polyhedron in 3-space with eight vertices can be transformed via a unimodular transformation into a specific form involving two adjacent lattice planes. The vertices lie on these planes, and the structure allows for a weak but useful version of convexity in integer programming problems. The paper demonstrates that for a 4×3 matrix A, there exists a family of parallel lattice planes such that if integral solutions exist on two planes, they also exist on all intermediate planes. This property enables solving three-variable integer programs by reducing them to two-variable problems on each plane, offering a form of decoupling significant for integer programming. The results are limited to n=3 due to the lack of generalization of Howe's theorem to higher dimensions.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The analysis and key results, particularly Howe's theorem, are specific to three-dimensional space and do not generalize to higher dimensions. The paper explicitly notes that the conjecture about integral polyhedra with 2^n vertices lying on two adjacent lattice planes fails for n=4, and the structure of integral polyhedra in higher dimensions remains unknown. Additionally, the method relies on a specialized theorem with no immediate extension beyond n=3.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future research should aim to extend the characterization of integral polyhedra to higher dimensions, despite the failure of the natural generalization of Howe's theorem. Investigating alternative forms of decoupling or convexity-like properties for integer programming problems in higher dimensions could yield significant advances. Further exploration of neighborhood systems and their relationship to global optimality in integer programming may also lead to new algorithmic approaches.

representative_papers.abstract: Jack Edmonds developed a new way of looking at extremal combinatorial problems and applied his technique with great success to maximal-weight degree-constrained subgraphs. This paper applies Edmonds' approach to hamiltonian graphs, introducing 'comb inequalities' satisfied by characteristic functions of hamiltonian circuits but not explicit in standard integer programming formulations. Using linear programming duality, a new necessary condition for the existence of hamiltonian circuits is derived, which appears stronger than previously known conditions. The work also relates linear programming to hamiltonian circuits, continuing the line of research initiated by Dantzig, Fulkerson, and Johnson on the traveling salesman problem.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The paper notes that while weakly hamiltonian functions provide a powerful framework, the facets of the corresponding polytope are complex—illustrated by the Petersen graph, where the inequality f·X ≤ 9 defines a facet despite being non-trivial. This complexity contrasts sharply with Edmonds' simpler facets in matching theory, suggesting inherent difficulty in characterizing hamiltonian structures via linear programming. Additionally, the elementary closure of inequalities is introduced as a tool, but its practical utility remains limited due to computational challenges.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future research could focus on refining the comb inequalities and exploring their computational efficiency in detecting non-hamiltonicity. Further investigation into the structure of the elementary closure of inequalities may yield deeper insights into the hierarchy of valid constraints. Extending the results to broader classes of graphs or developing algorithmic applications based on weakly hamiltonian functions would be valuable. Additionally, studying the relationship between weakly hamiltonian graphs and other graph properties, such as higher cyclability or toughness, could lead to stronger sufficient conditions for hamiltonicity.

representative_papers.abstract: We examine the single-item lot-sizing problem with Wagner-Whitin costs over an $n$ period horizon, i.e. $p_{t} + h_{t} \geqslant p_{t+1}$ for $t = 1, \dots, n-1$ , where $p_{t}, h_{t}$ are the unit production and storage costs in period $t$ respectively, so it always pays to produce as late as possible. We describe integral polyhedra whose solution as linear programs solve the uncapacitated problem (ULS), the uncapacitated problem with backlogging (BLS), the uncapacitated problem with startup costs (ULSS) and the constant capacity problem (CLS), respectively. The polyhedra, extended formulations and separation algorithms are much simpler than in the general cost case. In particular for models ULS and ULSS the polyhedra in the original space have only $\mathrm{O}(n^2)$ facets as opposed to $\mathrm{O}(2^n)$ in the general case. For CLS and BLS no explicit polyhedral descriptions are known for the general case in the original space. Here we exhibit polyhedra with $\mathrm{O}(2^n)$ facets having an $\mathrm{O}(n^2\log n)$ separation algorithm for CLS and $\mathrm{O}(n^3)$ for BLS, as well as extended formulations with $\mathrm{O}(n^2)$ constraints in both cases, $\mathrm{O}(n^2)$ variables for CLS and $\mathrm{O}(n)$ variables for BLS.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The analysis is restricted to the special case of Wagner-Whitin costs, where $p_t + h_t' - p_{t+1} \geqslant 0$. This condition simplifies the problem structure significantly compared to the general cost case. The authors note that for the CLS and BLS models, explicit polyhedral descriptions for the general cost case are not known. The introduction also mentions a 'negative result for the lot-sizing in series model', indicating the presented methods do not extend to that particular problem.
representative_papers.future_work_text: The paper examines two extensions to the core models presented: the inclusion of 'upper bound constraints on stocks, and limits on the number of production periods'.

domain_snapshot.development_history: The technical evolution in polyhedral structures and optimization over the past decade shows a progression from structural representations and lower bounds toward more refined, stability-aware, and computation-sensitive techniques that exploit polyhedral geometry inside broader convex-optimization frameworks. Earlier work emphasized representational efficiency and fundamental limits: extension complexity results (2017) quantified how hard families of polytopes are to represent via linear or semidefinite extended formulations, linking geometric separation (e.g., Hausdorff distance) and family size to unavoidable formulation size, thereby formalizing intrinsic barriers to compact modeling. In parallel, polynomial/sum-of-squares viewpoints (2017) studied certificates of nonnegativity over discrete polyhedral domains (k-subset hypercubes), developing symmetry-exploiting SOS constructions that complement polyhedral relaxations and help explain when stronger-than-linear relaxations are needed. Moving forward, research increasingly integrated polyhedral substructure into conic optimization algorithms: facial reduction with partial polyhedrality (2018) introduced methods that adaptively detect minimal faces while leveraging polyhedral faces inside general cones, addressing degeneracy/infeasibility and improving practical robustness in conic linear programs. More recent work focused on mixed-integer geometry and stability/variational properties. Lattice closures (2019) generalized integrality enforcement by taking convex hulls of points satisfying multiple linear integrality conditions, refining the toolkit for generating strong closures/cuts beyond classical split and Chvátal-Gomory paradigms. representative_papers.l2_label: Strong Formulations for Mixed Integer Programming
representative_papers.abstract: Chvátal introduced the idea of viewing cutting planes as a system for proving that every integral solution of a given set of linear inequalities satisfies another given linear inequality. This viewpoint has proven to be very useful in many studies of combinatorial and integer programming problems. The basic ingredient in these cutting-plane proofs is that for a polyhedron $P$ and integral vector $w$ , if $\max(wx|x \in P,wx\text{integer}\} = t$ , then $wx \leqslant t$ is valid for all integral vectors in $P$ . We consider the variant of this step where the requirement that $wx$ be integer may be replaced by the requirement that $\bar{w}x$ be integer for some other integral vector $\bar{w}$ . The cutting-plane proofs thus obtained may be seen either as an abstraction of Gomory's mixed integer cutting-plane technique or as a proof version of a simple class of the disjunctive cutting planes studied by Balas and Jeroslow. Our main result is that for a given polyhedron $P$ , the set of vectors that satisfy every cutting plane for $P$ with respect to a specified subset of integer variables is again a polyhedron. This allows us to obtain a finite recursive procedure for generating the mixed integer hull of a polyhedron, analogous to the process of repeatedly taking Chvátal closures in the integer programming case. These results are illustrated with a number of examples from combinatorial optimization. Our work can be seen as a continuation of that of Nemhauser and Wolsey on mixed integer cutting planes.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The split closure cannot get 'stuck' in the sense of Example 1, but although $\hat{P} \neq P$, the difference between these two polyhedra may become arbitrarily small after repeated split closure operations, as shown in Example 2. Specifically, for a polyhedron $P$ defined as the convex hull of certain points including $(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}, \varepsilon)$, the split closure $\hat{P}$ may exclude no integral points but still fail to converge to the mixed integer hull $P_{\mathrm{I}(x)}$ in finite steps due to the diminishing gap caused by rational approximations.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Further research is needed to determine whether repeated split closures eventually yield the mixed integer hull $P_{\mathrm{I}(x)}$ in finite time, despite cases where convergence is arbitrarily slow. Investigating conditions under which finite convergence occurs—such as structural properties of the polyhedron or constraints on variable types—would extend the applicability of split cuts. Additionally, computational experiments and algorithmic implementations of the split closure procedure could assess practical performance in mixed integer programming solvers.

representative_papers.abstract: In this paper we use facets of simple mixed-integer sets with three variables to derive a parametric family of valid inequalities for general mixed-integer sets. We call these inequalities two-step MIR inequalities as they can be derived by applying the simple mixed-integer rounding (MIR) principle of Wolsey (1998) twice. representative_papers.abstract: Linear programs with joint probabilistic constraints (PCLP) are difficult to solve because the feasible region is not convex. We consider a special case of PCLP in which only the right-hand side is random and this random vector has a finite distribution. We give a mixed-integer programming formulation for this special case and study the relaxation corresponding to a single row of the probabilistic constraint. We obtain two strengthened formulations. As a byproduct of this analysis, we obtain new results for the previously studied mixing set, subject to an additional knapsack inequality. We present computational results which indicate that by using our strengthened formulations, instances that are considerably larger than have been considered before can be solved to optimality.

representative_papers.abstract: An outer-approximation algorithm is presented for solving mixed-integer nonlinear programming problems of a particular class. Linearity of the integer (or discrete) variables, and convexity of the nonlinear functions involving continuous variables are the main features in the underlying mathematical structure. Based on principles of decomposition, outer-approximation and relaxation, the proposed algorithm effectively exploits the structure of the problems, and consists of solving an alternating finite sequence of nonlinear programming subproblems and relaxed versions of a mixed-integer linear master program. Convergence and optimality properties of the algorithm are presented, as well as a general discussion on its implementation. Numerical results are reported for several example problems to illustrate the potential of the proposed algorithm for programs in the class addressed in this paper. Finally, a theoretical comparison with generalized Benders decomposition is presented on the lower bounds predicted by the relaxed master programs.

representative_papers.abstract: We investigate strong inequalities for mixed 0-1 integer programs derived from flow cover inequalities. Flow cover inequalities are usually not facet defining and need to be lifted to obtain stronger inequalities. However, because of the sequential nature of the standard lifting techniques and the complexity of the optimization problems that have to be solved to obtain lifting coefficients, lifting of flow cover inequalities is computationally very demanding. We present a computationally efficient way to lift flow cover inequalities based on sequence independent lifting techniques and give computational results that show the effectiveness of our lifting procedures.

representative_papers.abstract: The purpose of this paper is to present sufficient conditions for the existence of optimal solutions to integer and mixed-integer programming problems in the absence of upper bounds on the integer variables. Some computational implications of these results are also given.

representative_papers.l2_label: Strong Formulations for Mixed Integer Programming
representative_papers.abstract: Mixed-integer rounding (MIR) inequalities play a central role in the development of strong cutting planes for mixed-integer programs. In this paper, we investigate how known MIR inequalities can be combined in order to generate new strong valid inequalities. Given a mixed-integer region $S$ and a collection of valid "base" mixed-integer inequalities, we develop a procedure for generating new valid inequalities for $S$. The starting point of our procedure is to consider the MIR inequalities related with the base inequalities. For any subset of these MIR inequalities, we generate two new inequalities by combining or "mixing" them. We show that the new inequalities are strong in the sense that they fully describe the convex hull of a special mixed-integer region associated with the base inequalities. We discuss how the mixing procedure can be used to obtain new classes of strong valid inequalities for various mixed-integer programming problems. In particular, we present examples for production planning, capacitated facility location, capacitated network design, and multiple knapsack problems. We also present preliminary computational results using the mixing procedure to tighten the formulation of some difficult integer programs. Finally we study some extensions of this mixing procedure.
representative_papers.future_work_text: We study some extensions of this mixing procedure that produce stronger valid inequalities when the base inequalities have additional structure. Future work includes further exploration of the separation problem associated with the mixed MIR inequalities and identifying practical ways to implement the procedure in large-scale optimization settings.
