representative_papers.abstract: We present an algorithm for large-scale unconstrained optimization based on Newton's method. In large-scale optimization, solving the Newton equations at each iteration can be expensive and may not be justified when far from a solution. Instead, an inaccurate solution to the Newton equations is computed using a conjugate gradient method. The resulting algorithm is shown to have strong convergence properties and has the unusual feature that the asymptotic convergence rate is a user specified parameter which can be set to anything between linear and quadratic convergence. Some numerical results on a 916 variable test problem are given. Finally, we contrast the computational behavior of our algorithm with Newton's method and that of a nonlinear conjugate gradient algorithm.

(J Bank Finance 30:583-605, 2006) which proposes a smoothing method to deal with nonsmoothness in a conditional value-at-risk problem, we consider a smoothing scheme for a general class of nonsmooth stochastic problems. Assuming that a smoothed problem is solved by a sample average approximation method, we investigate the convergence of stationary points of the smoothed sample average approximation problem as sample size increases and show that w.p.1 accumulation points of the stationary points of the approximation problem are weak stationary points of their counterparts of the true problem. Moreover, under some metric regularity conditions, we obtain an error bound on approximate stationary points. The convergence result is applied to a conditional value-at-risk problem and an inventory control problem.

representative_papers.abstract: We consider the famous Hamiltonian cycle problem (HCP) embedded in a Markov decision process (MDP). More specifically, we consider the HCP as an optimisation problem over the space of occupation measures induced by the MDP's stationary policies. In recent years, this approach to the HCP has led to a number of alternative formulations and algorithmic approaches. In this paper, we focus on a specific embedding, because of the work of Feinberg. We present a "branch-and-fix" type algorithm that solves the HCP. At each branch of the algorithm, only a linear program needs to be solved and the dimensions of the successive linear programs are shrinking rather than expanding. Because the nodes of the branch-and-fix tree correspond to specially structured 1-randomised policies, we characterise the latter. This characterisation indicates that the total number of such policies is significantly smaller than the subset of all 1-randomised policies. Finally, we present some numerical results.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The algorithm's performance, while effective for many instances, may vary depending on graph structure; non-Hamiltonian graphs, though handled well, still pose challenges in certain cases. Additionally, the method relies on specific assumptions about the initial distribution and discount factor, which may limit generalizability to other MDP formulations.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future research could explore extending the algorithm to undirected graphs or incorporating additional structural constraints to further reduce branching. Investigating hybrid approaches combining this method with heuristic or metaheuristic techniques may improve scalability for larger instances. Moreover, theoretical analysis of convergence properties under broader conditions remains an open direction.

domain_snapshot.development_history: Early foundations (circa 2011) focused on tractable approximations and scalable first-order algorithms for large, structured optimization problems under uncertainty. On the modeling side, two-stage adaptive robust optimization analyzed the computational power and structural limits of common decision rules (notably affine recourse), clarifying when tractability comes at a significant optimality cost and when assumptions (e.g., nonnegativity of RHS/objective) restrict expressiveness. In parallel, stochastic programming theory developed stationarity/optimality function frameworks to define and verify solution concepts for expectation-based objectives and constraints, including nonlinear and potentially nonconvex cases, connecting stochastic programs to semi-infinite optimization notions. On the algorithmic side, large-scale optimization advanced via limited-memory and block-coordinate methods: Barzilai–Borwein-inspired limited-memory steepest descent targeted scalability with minimal storage, while block coordinate gradient descent for composite/separable convex objectives provided convergence guarantees under strengthened Lipschitz/bounded-level-set assumptions and demonstrated empirical efficiency for high-dimensional problems (e.g., covariance selection). By 2017, DRO matured toward richer ambiguity sets and more explicit duality-based solution methods: matrix moment-constrained DRO used Lagrange duality to reformulate inner distributional maximization into semi-infinite programs and employed cutting-plane schemes, emphasizing strong duality conditions and iterative constraint generation to handle infinitely many distributional constraints. Overall, the trajectory moves from (i) tractable but restrictive policy/uncertainty representations and generic large-scale solvers, toward (ii) duality-driven DRO reformulations with more expressive ambiguity sets and specialized decomposition/cutting-plane algorithms, while continuing to rely on scalable first-order/coordinate/limited-memory optimization machinery to make these formulations computationally viable.

gaps: Strong duality and regularity for expressive DRO ambiguity sets
Scalability of semi-infinite/cutting-plane DRO in large dimensions
Policy restrictiveness vs. tractability in adaptive/robust designs
future_works: Regularity-robust DRO algorithms with certified primal-dual correctness under weak constraint qualifications
Scalable decomposition integrating cutting planes with limited-memory/coordinate optimization for large DRO masters
Beyond affine policies: tractable higher-expressivity decision rules with performance guarantees

representative_papers.abstract: The solution of the Chinese postman problem using matching theory is given. The convex hull of integer solutions is described as a linear programming polyhedron. This polyhedron is used to show that a good algorithm gives an optimum solution. The algorithm is a specialization of the more general $b$-matching blossom algorithm. Algorithms for finding Euler tours and related problems are also discussed.

representative_papers.abstract: A zero-one matrix is called perfect if the polytope of the associated set packing problem has integral vertices only. By this definition, all totally unimodular zero-one matrices are perfect. In this paper we give a characterization of perfect zero-one matrices in terms of forbidden submatrices. Perfect zero-one matrices are closely related to perfect graphs and constitute a generalization of balanced matrices as introduced by C. Berge. Furthermore, the results obtained here bear on an unsolved problem in graph theory, the strong perfect graph conjecture, also due to C. Berge.

representative_papers.abstract: An odd chain packing $P$ in a graph is an edge-disjoint collection of odd length chains (and even cycles) such that each node is the endpoint of at most one chain of $P$. We define the ocp partition number of a graph $G$ as the smallest $k$ such that the edge set $G$ can be partitioned into $k$ odd chain packings. A min-max theorem is given for bipartite graphs: it is an analogue of the second theorem of König. Some remarks on the corresponding covering problem are given and some other odd chain problems are mentioned.
representative_papers.limitation_text: It seems more difficult to characterize the graphs $G$ for which $q_0(G) \leqslant 2$. The numbers of edges in the ocp's can usually not be balanced; for instance the graph $G$ in Fig. 1 has $q_0(G) = 2$; in any partition into 2 ocp's we have 6 edges in one ocp and 1 in the other.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Some other odd chain problems are mentioned. Further research is needed to characterize graphs with ocp partition number at most 2, and to explore extensions of the Berge, Norman, Rabin theorem.

representative_papers.abstract: We introduce orbitopes as the convex hulls of $0/1$-matrices that are lexicographically maximal subject to a group acting on the columns. Special cases are packing and partitioning orbitopes, which arise from restrictions to matrices with at most or exactly one 1-entry in each row, respectively. The goal of investigating these polytopes is to gain insight into ways of breaking certain symmetries in integer programs by adding constraints, e.g., for a well-known formulation of the graph coloring problem. We provide a thorough polyhedral investigation of packing and partitioning orbitopes for the cases in which the group acting on the columns is the cyclic group or the symmetric group. Our main results are complete linear inequality descriptions of these polytopes by facet-defining inequalities. For the cyclic group case, the descriptions turn out to be totally unimodular, while for the symmetric group case, both the description and the proof are more involved. The associated separation problems can be solved in linear time.
representative_papers.future_work_text: While this work lays the theoretical foundations on orbitopes, a thorough computational investigation of the practical usefulness of the results will be the subject of further studies (see also the remarks in Sect. 5).

representative_papers.abstract: A D matrix is a real square matrix M such that for every q the linear complementarity problem: Find w and z satisfying w = q + Mz , w >= 0 , z >= 0 , w^Tz = 0 , has a solution. We characterize the class of completely-D matrices, defined here as the class of D-matrices all of whose nonempty principal submatrices are also D-matrices.
representative_papers.limitation_text: If Van der Heyden's algorithm is limited to the class of matrices for which it has been shown to work, then it is definitely less powerful than Lemke's [9], and [3], for the latter will solve problems based on a much larger class than D-tilde. But is van der Heyden's algorithm actually limited to D-tilde? At present the answer seems unknown.
representative_papers.future_work_text: The second open question concerns a class of matrices which could be called completely-Z_0 or D_0-bar-matrices. Such matrices have the property that they and all their (proper) principal submatrices belong to Z_0 (formerly called K), i.e. (q, M) is solvable provided (1) and (2) are consistent. As examples of D_0-bar-matrices, we can cite copositive-plus matrices and X-matrices. (These are defined in [10]). The second open question is: What is D_0-bar? It appears that the characterization will be harder to find than that for the corresponding class D-bar. Both questions are presently under investigation.

representative_papers.abstract: This comment provides a slight generalization of Theorem 1 from M.C. Cheng's paper regarding conditions ensuring that a nonbasic variable remains nonbasic in an optimal basic solution. It also presents a counterexample to Theorem 2, which claimed that certain basic variables would remain basic in an optimal solution, demonstrating that the theorem does not hold in general. The analysis highlights issues with the stated conditions and suggests a corrected dualized version would yield valid results.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The counterexample shows that Theorem 2 in Cheng's paper is invalid, as it fails to guarantee that a basic variable remains basic in an optimal solution under the proposed conditions. Specifically, variable $x_4$ satisfies the conditions of Theorem 2 in Table 2 but becomes nonbasic in the optimal solution (Table 5), indicating a flaw in the theorem's logic or assumptions.
representative_papers.future_work_text: A rigorous dualization of the theorems presented in this paper could lead to corrected and valid conditions for preserving basis structure across optimal solutions. Future work should focus on refining criteria for maintaining basic and nonbasic variables in optimal solutions, particularly under degeneracy, and exploring generalized duality-based approaches to ensure correctness.

representative_papers.abstract: The concept of line perfection of a graph is defined so that a simple graph is line perfect if and only if its line graph is perfect in the usual sense. Line perfect graphs are characterized as those which contain no odd cycles of size larger than 3. Two well-known theorems of König for bipartite graphs are shown to hold also for line perfect graphs; this extension provides a reinterpretation of the content of these theorems.
representative_papers.limitation_text: The paper focuses on graphs without odd cycles larger than three, limiting generalization to broader classes of graphs. The results rely on structural properties specific to line perfect graphs and do not extend directly to arbitrary graphs beyond this class.
representative_papers.future_work_text: Future work could explore extending the characterization of line perfect graphs to other graph classes, investigating connections with the Strong Perfect Graph Conjecture, and developing efficient algorithms for identifying line perfect graphs or computing maximum matchings in such graphs.

representative_papers.abstract: We study facets of the cut cone $C_n$, i.e., the cone of dimension $ rac{1}{2} n(n - 1)$ generated by the cuts of the complete graph on $n$ vertices. The study of the facets of the cut cone is equivalent in some sense to the study of the facets of the cut polytope. We present several operations on facets and, in particular, a 'lifting' procedure for constructing facets of $C_{n + 1}$ from given facets of $C_n$. After reviewing hypermetric valid inequalities, we describe the new class of cycle inequalities and prove the facet property for several subclasses. The new class of parachute facets is developed and other known facets and valid inequalities are presented.
representative_papers.future_work_text: We suggest that hypermetric and cycle inequalities belong to a larger class of valid inequalities arising from integers $b_i$ with suitably chosen sum; these ideas will be further developed in a follow-up work [24].

domain_snapshot.development_history: Early work relevant to graph-structured game analysis was driven by polyhedral and algorithmic foundations for discrete decision problems: studies on Chvátal-Gomory style procedures (e.g., small Chvátal rank) formalized how constraint structure controls the complexity of deriving tight integer descriptions, while related geometric and combinatorial analyses (e.g., vectors-in-a-box constructions and geometric properties enabling strongly polynomial simplex variants) clarified when structural regularities yield efficient optimization. By the mid-2010s, attention broadened toward scalability limits in nonlinear unconstrained binary optimization: strong methods existed for quadratic objectives, but the gap for higher-order nonlinearities highlighted the need for structure-exploiting representations and decomposition. In the early 2020s, this structural viewpoint increasingly intersected with cooperative game theory on graphs, exemplified by arboricity games that encode cost-sharing over graph covering problems; here, the “graph structure → optimization structure → game solution concepts” pipeline became explicit, focusing on allocations like the core and nucleolus derived from graph-defined cost functions. Overall, the technical evolution moved from general polyhedral/algorithmic tools for discrete optimization, to recognizing scalability barriers and the importance of exploitable structure, and finally to formal game-theoretic constructs whose solution concepts depend critically on graph-induced combinatorics and tractable optimization subroutines.

gaps: Scalable computation of cooperative solution concepts on large graphs
Lack of compact polyhedral characterizations for structured coalition spaces
Bridging higher-order nonlinear objective structure to graph-game primitives
future_works: Structure-aware nucleolus/core algorithms for graph-induced cost games via separation and decomposition
Polyhedral/extended-formulation study of allocation regions for graph games (core polytopes, least-core, and related relaxations)
Hybrid graph–pseudo-Boolean modeling to handle higher-order coalition synergies with controlled tractability
